Vowel harmony and rounding

A suffix takes its vowel from the last vowel of the word: front (e, ä, i, ö, ü) or back (a, o, u, y). In the course, A is a or e and Y is y or i. After a rounded vowel (o, ö, u, ü) in the first syllable, a Y in the second syllable is u or ü, unless it ends the word.

Last vowelPluralmy …his, her …
a, yA is a, Y is ykitap­larkitab­ymkitab­y
o, uA is a, Y is y or udost­lardost­umdost­y
e, ä, iA is e, Y is imekdep­lermekdeb­immekdeb­i
ö, üA is e, Y is i or ügöz­lergöz­ümgöz­i

Two endings have ä in front words: -ýÄr (gel­ýär, but al­ýar) and -rÄk (kiçi­räk).

Sound changes and buffer letters

  • Voicing: before a vowel, a final k, p or ç of a word of two or more syllables becomes g, b or j: kitap → kitab­y, çörek → çöreg­i, agaç → agaj­y. Most one-syllable words keep theirs (top­y), but those with a long vowel voice: at (name) → ad­ym, while at (horse) → at­ym. A final t voices in a few words: Aşgabad­a.
  • Vowel loss: some words lose their second vowel before a vowel: ogul → ogl­um, burun → burn­um, agyz → agz­y.
  • The dative after a vowel merges with it: Mary → Mar­a, okuwçy → okuwç­a, eje → ej­ä.
  • e becomes ä at the end of a word before some endings: eje → ej­ä; işlemek → işlä­p, işlä­r.
  • Buffer letters: after a vowel, -(n)Y, -(n)Yň and -(s)Y take n or s: okuwçy­n­y, okuwçy­n­yň, okuwçy­s­y; and a case after his, her or its takes an n: öý­ü­n­de, kitab­y­n­a.
  • No apostrophe, names included: Aşgabat­da, Merdan­yň. A number takes a hyphen: 1991-nji ýylda.

The cases

Turkmen has no words for in, to or from: an ending on the noun does the job, and the d of -dA and -dAn never changes. The plural -lAr comes first, then the possessive, then the case: öý­ler­imiz­de (in our houses). With is the word bilen, after the noun: Aýna bilen.

Caseöýkitapmekdepokuwçy

Dativeto, toward-Aöý­ekitab­amekdeb­eokuwç­a
Accusativethe (a specific object)-(n)Yöý­ikitab­ymekdeb­iokuwçy­n­y
Locativein, at, on-dAöý­dekitap­damekdep­deokuwçy­da

“To be”

In the present, “to be” is usually not said: put the two words side by side, with the subject. däl makes it negative; the question ending -mY is written onto the word. In careful style the third person takes -dYr: ol talypdyr; formal writing gives the other persons -dYr with the endings too: talypdyryn, talypdyrsyň…

PersonI'm a studentI'm notAm I?I was
menmen talypmen talyp dälmen talypmy?men talypdym
sensen talypsen talyp dälsen talypmy?sen talypdyň
olol talypol talyp dälol talypmy?ol talypdy
bizbiz talypbiz talyp dälbiz talypmy?biz talypdyk
sizsiz talypsiz talyp dälsiz talypmy?siz talypdyňyz
olarolar talypolar talyp dälolar talypmy?olar talypdylar

There is, there isn't: bar, ýok; in the past bardy, ýokdy. So it is, I hear: Ol talyp eken.

Participles: the boy who is reading, the book I read

Everything that describes a noun comes before it, with the participle last. When someone else does the action, the possessive goes on the noun.

SuffixExampleMeaning
-ýAnkitap okaýan oglanthe boy who is reading a book
-Andüýn gelen myhmanthe guest who came yesterday
-An + possessivemeniň okan kitabymthe book I read
-jAk + possessivemeniň okajak kitabymthe book I'm going to read
-mAdYkgörmedik ýera place I haven't seen
-dYgYOnuň gelendigini bilýärin.I know that he came.

Word order

  • The verb comes last: subject, object, verb. Men çaý içýärin. (I drink tea.)
  • Time and place come before an object without an ending, which sits right before the verb: Men her gün çörek alýaryn. (I buy bread every day.)
  • The word right before the verb is in focus: Çöregi men alýaryn. (I'm the one buying the bread.)
  • Adjectives, possessors and descriptions come before the noun: bazarda haly satýan adam (the man who sells carpets at the bazaar).
  • Postpositions come after their noun, and after a pronoun in the genitive: meniň bilen (with me), seniň üçin (for you).
